p.src: Let the Mathematics Test the Intuition

u.src: Let the Mathematics Test the Intuition
en: Let the Mathematics Test the Intuition

p.src: Thermodynamics has a peculiar reputation. Its calculus is elementary, yet the choice of what to differentiate and what to hold fixed can be remarkably subtle. Our problem is deliberately narrow: calculate the pressure of an ideal gas. The route to that answer, however, is intended to be general enough for systems in which the familiar molecular picture is no longer reliable.

en: Thermodynamics has a peculiar reputation. Its calculus is elementary, yet the choice of what to differentiate and what to hold fixed can be remarkably subtle. Our problem is deliberately narrow: calculate the pressure of an ideal gas. The route to that answer, however, is intended to be general enough for systems in which the familiar molecular picture is no longer reliable.

p.src:
The kinetic story is easy to tell. Molecules strike a wall and reverse the normal component of their momentum. Momentum delivered per unit time gives the force, and force per unit area gives the pressure. We already know that the mean kinetic energy per molecule in three dimensions is $\left\langle \frac{p^2}{2m}\right\rangle=\frac{3}{2}T
 \qquad (k_B=1).$ With an isotropic velocity distribution one can estimate the collision rate, the momentum transfer in each collision, and the resulting pressure.

p.src: But the wall itself seems to spoil isotropy. Why should molecules very near the boundary have the same distribution of speeds and directions as molecules deep in the interior? In equilibrium they do, to the accuracy relevant here, but that conclusion should follow from statistical mechanics rather than be smuggled into the calculation as intuition. Collisions among the molecules make the kinetic argument still less transparent. The noninteracting gas is easy precisely because it is an unusually simple system.

p.src: There are occasions in physics when the safest procedure is to suppress the picture temporarily and ride the mathematics. One identifies the quantity to be found, manipulates the general relations, and waits until a recognizable formula appears. Intuition returns at the end, but then the mathematics is testing the intuition rather than the other way around. The pleasure of thermodynamics lies in the surprising relations that emerge from this procedure.

p.src: The desired relation is an equation of state, $P=P(T,V,N),$ where $N$ is the amount of material, $T$ the temperature, and $V$ the volume. A satisfactory derivation should continue to make sense when the particles interact, or when the material is a liquid, plasma, or solid. Only the final evaluation of the partition function will specialize to an ideal gas.

p.src: Entropy and the Helmholtz Free Energy

u.src: Entropy and the Helmholtz Free Energy
en: Entropy and the Helmholtz Free Energy

p.src:
Begin by retrieving the canonical formulas that will be needed later. For microstates labelled by $i$, $\begin{aligned}
 S&=-\sum_i p_i\log p_i,\\
 p_i&=\frac{e^{-\beta E_i}}{Z},\\
 Z&=\sum_i e^{-\beta E_i}.
 \end{aligned}$ The logarithm of the probability is $\log p_i=-\beta E_i-\log Z.$ Substitution into the entropy gives $\begin{aligned}
 S
 &=-\sum_i p_i\log p_i \notag\\
 &=\beta\sum_i p_iE_i+\log Z\sum_i p_i \notag\\
 &=\beta E+\log Z.
 \end{aligned}$ Here $E=\sum_i p_iE_i$ is the mean energy.

p.src:
In the energy units used through most of the lecture, $\beta=1/T$. Multiplying  by $T$ and rearranging gives $E-TS=-T\log Z.$ The combination on the left occurs so often that it deserves a name: $A\equiv E-TS,
 \qquad
 A=-T\log Z.$ It is the Helmholtz free energy. The name is less important at this moment than the identity itself; we shall need the identity when pressure is converted into a derivative of the partition function.

p.src: Control Parameters and Their Responses

u.src: Control Parameters and Their Responses
en: Control Parameters and Their Responses

p.src: A control parameter is a macroscopic quantity that an experimenter can change from outside. Moving a piston changes the volume without manipulating individual molecules. Applied electric and magnetic fields are other examples. In a more general ensemble, the number of particles can also be allowed to change.

p.src: Thermodynamic variables naturally come in conjugate pairs. Volume is the control parameter in the present problem, and pressure is its response. We change $V$; the pressure tells us how the system energetically resists that change. Later the derivative of the energy will make this pairing precise.

For the next argument, regard energy and entropy as dependent functions of two independently adjustable variables: $E=E(T,V),
 \qquad
 S=S(T,V).$ Temperature and volume provide coordinates on a thermodynamic state space. Energy and entropy assign numbers to every equilibrium point in that space.

p.src: The derivative we ultimately need is unusual: $\left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial V}\right)_S.$ Although $T$ and $V$ are the independent coordinates, this derivative asks us to change $V$ while constraining the dependent function $S(T,V)$ to remain constant. It is a derivative along a curve in the $(T,V)$-plane, not along a coordinate axis.

p.src: Piston Work and the Adiabatic Condition

u.src: Piston Work and the Adiabatic Condition
en: Piston Work and the Adiabatic Condition

p.src: We now give the derivative a physical meaning. Consider a piston with cross-sectional area $\mathcal A$. If it moves outward by $dx$, then $dV=\mathcal A\,dx.$ The gas exerts force $P\mathcal A$ on the piston, so the work done by the gas is $\delta W_{\mathrm{by}}=P\mathcal A\,dx=P\,dV.$ If no heat enters the gas, energy conservation gives $dE=-P\,dV.$ The sign is physical: during expansion the gas raises or accelerates the piston, and its own energy decreases.

p.src: Two qualifications are essential. The piston must move slowly enough for the system to remain arbitrarily close to equilibrium, and the walls must be insulated so that energy is not supplied as heat. A rapid pull can be so fast that no molecule reaches the receding piston during the motion. A rapid compression launches shock waves. Neither process is represented by a sequence of equilibrium states.

p.src: From Adiabatic Energy to the Partition Function

u.src: From Adiabatic Energy to the Partition Function
en: From Adiabatic Energy to the Partition Function

p.src:
The physical formula  is not yet the easy one to calculate. Canonical statistical mechanics naturally supplies functions of temperature, because $T$ appears directly in the Boltzmann weight. The calculus lemma converts the awkward fixed-entropy derivative into that calculational language: $\begin{aligned}
 P
 &=
 -\left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial V}\right)_T
 +
 \left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial S}\right)_V
 \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T.
 \end{aligned}$ At fixed volume the first law gives $dE=T\,dS$, and therefore $\left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial S}\right)_V=T.$ Thus $P=
 -\left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial V}\right)_T
 +
 T\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T.$

More generally, every external control parameter has a conjugate response obtained by differentiating an appropriate thermodynamic potential. The partition function packages many such responses: differentiating $\log Z$ with respect to $\beta$ gives energy, while differentiating it with respect to volume gives pressure.

p.src: The Ideal-Gas Equation of State

u.src: The Ideal-Gas Equation of State
en: The Ideal-Gas Equation of State

p.src:
Only now specialize to $N$ noninteracting particles. With the classical phase-space normalization retained, $Z_N=
 \frac{1}{N!h^{3N}}
 \int d^{3N}q\,d^{3N}p\,
 \exp\!\left[
 -\beta\sum_{a=1}^{N}\frac{\mathbf p_a^2}{2m}
 \right].$ There are $3N$ position coordinates and $3N$ momentum coordinates. The Hamiltonian is independent of position, so every particle contributes one factor of the container volume: $Z_N=
 \frac{V^N}{N!h^{3N}}I_p(\beta),$ where the entire momentum integral $I_p(\beta)$ is independent of $V$.

 \right].$ There are $3N$ position coordinates and $3N$ momentum coordinates. The Hamiltonian is independent of position, so every particle contributes one factor of the container volume: $Z_N=

p.src:
Taking a logarithm separates the volume dependence: $\log Z_N
 =
 N\log V-\log N!-3N\log h+\log I_p(\beta).$ The factors $1/N!$, $h^{-3N}$, and $I_p(\beta)$ are all independent of volume. They matter for absolute entropy and other questions, but not for this particular derivative. Hence $\left(\frac{\partial\log Z_N}{\partial V}\right)_T
 =\frac{N}{V}.$ Equation  immediately gives $P=\frac{NT}{V},
 \qquad
 \boxed{PV=NT}.$

p.src: Variance and Standard Deviation

u.src: Variance and Standard Deviation
en: Variance and Standard Deviation

p.src:
For a random variable $x$ with $\langle x\rangle=0$, a measure of the distribution’s width is $\langle x^2\rangle$. For a general distribution, shift the variable by its mean: $\delta x=x-\langle x\rangle.$ Its mean vanishes, $\langle\delta x\rangle
 =
 \langle x\rangle-\langle x\rangle=0,$ and its mean square is $\begin{aligned}
 (\Delta x)^2
 &\equiv
 \left\langle\left(x-\langle x\rangle\right)^2\right\rangle \notag\\
 &=
 \langle x^2\rangle
 -2\langle x\rangle^2
 +\langle x\rangle^2 \notag\\
 &=
 \langle x^2\rangle-\langle x\rangle^2.
 \end{aligned}$ This is the variance. Its positive square root $\Delta x$ is the standard deviation.

p.src: Energy Moments from the Partition Function

u.src: Energy Moments from the Partition Function
en: Energy Moments from the Partition Function

p.src:
For the canonical ensemble, $\begin{aligned}
 \langle E\rangle
 &=
 \frac{1}{Z}\sum_i E_i e^{-\beta E_i} \notag\\
 &=
 -\frac{1}{Z}\frac{\partial Z}{\partial\beta}
 =
 -\frac{\partial\log Z}{\partial\beta}.
 \end{aligned}$ Multiplication by one factor of $E_i$ is produced by one negative $\beta$-derivative. A second derivative generates $E_i^2$: $\langle E^2\rangle
 =
 \frac{1}{Z}\sum_i E_i^2e^{-\beta E_i}
 =
 \frac{1}{Z}\frac{\partial^2 Z}{\partial\beta^2}.$ The energy variance is consequently $\begin{aligned}
 (\Delta E)^2
 &=
 \langle E^2\rangle-\langle E\rangle^2 \notag\\
 &=
 \frac{1}{Z}\frac{\partial^2Z}{\partial\beta^2}
 -
 \frac{1}{Z^2}
 \left(\frac{\partial Z}{\partial\beta}\right)^2 \notag\\
 &=
 \frac{\partial^2\log Z}{\partial\beta^2}
 =
 -\frac{\partial\langle E\rangle}{\partial\beta}.
 \end{aligned}$ Once again, a complicated-looking observable becomes a derivative of $\log Z$.

p.src: For ordinary extensive matter, $C_V$ is proportional to $N$, so $(\Delta E)^2$ is proportional to $N$ and $\Delta E$ to $\sqrt{N}$. The mean energy itself is proportional to $N$. Therefore $\frac{\Delta E}{\langle E\rangle}\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}.$ Macroscopic relative fluctuations are tiny, while microscopic samples display them directly. The appearance of $k_B$ in  marks this connection between thermodynamic observables and molecular discreteness; equivalently, it connects macroscopic units to Avogadro-scale counting.

Pressure and fluctuations have now emerged from the same object: $P=T\left(\frac{\partial\log Z}{\partial V}\right)_T,
 \qquad
 (\Delta E)^2=\frac{\partial^2\log Z}{\partial\beta^2}.$ This is the central lesson. Once the correct constraints are identified, the partition function does not merely normalize probabilities. Its derivatives organize the measurable thermodynamics of the system.
